_layer: REKORD layer 3: source term / release to atmosphere
_note: A RANGE, not a number. Every entry carries the released activity as quoted and, where layer 2 can support it, the fraction of the core inventory that represents. Where the fraction is not derivable the entry says so instead of guessing.
_method: Released activities are quoted from IAEA Pub1239 Table 3.1, not modelled. Release fractions are released_activity / core_activity, with core_activity computed from layer-2 atoms and the layer-1 decay constant. No release fraction is fitted to anything.
_sourcePolicy: Russian/Soviet primary sources are preferred. For the release itself no Russian primary tabulation was available in this environment, so the IAEA consolidation is used and labelled. It is a second-best source under this project's policy and should be replaced when a Russian source is obtained.

_releaseWindow.uncertaintyMeaning: each daily release rate is uncertain by +/-50%
_releaseWindow.source: IAEA Pub1239 (2006) s.3.1.1 and Fig. 3.1: releases continued until 6 May 1986; the daily rate is uncertain by +/-50%; the rate falls to 0.002-0.006 EBq/d during the cooldown period

_fuelReleaseFraction.source: IAEA Pub1239 (2006) s.3.1.2, quoting Kashparov et al., Sci. Total Environ. 317 (2003) 105-119: release fraction of Sr-90, Eu-154, Pu-238, Pu-239/240 and Am-241, and therefore of the nuclear fuel itself, deposited outside the site = 1.5% +/- 0.5%, 'which is half that of earlier estimates'
_fuelReleaseFraction.earlierSource: The earlier estimate the same sentence halves: ~3%, the value used by INSAG-1 (1986) and still quoted in many secondary accounts
_fuelReleaseFraction.note: This is the quantity every refractory nuclide's release depends on. It moved by a factor of two between INSAG-1 and Kashparov, which is the single largest reason the source term is a range.

_caesiumRevision.note: Pub1239 s.3.1.1: the early airborne-radiometric estimate of Cs-137 deposited in the former USSR was about 40 PBq; the current estimate is about twice that, 80 PBq. Recorded because it is a worked example of the source term being revised by 2x on measurement, not on modelling.

_layer2LimitsExplained: Deriving a release fraction needs a correct core activity. The cross-check against Table 3.1 found three classes of nuclide for which layer 2 cannot supply one, and they are listed rather than papered over: (1) ACTIVATION PRODUCTS. Layer 2 is a fission-product inventory; it contains no nuclide above Z=70, so Pu, Np, Am, Cm and Co are absent. Table 3.1's seven actinide entries therefore carry a quoted released activity and no fraction. (2) ISOMER FEEDING. A decay branch records a mode and a branching ratio but not a daughter level, so beta decay into an excited state cannot be represented. Te-129m is fed by Sb-129 and is starved by 3-4 orders of magnitude as a result. (3) NEUTRON CAPTURE. Layer 2 solves decay chains with fission as the source and models no (n,g) reaction, so Cs-134 (made from Cs-133 by capture) and Cs-136 are under-produced. These are layer-2 defects that layer 3 exposes; fixing them belongs to layer 2, not to a fudge factor here.
_notInThisFile: No dose, no transport, no deposition, no release rate per nuclide. Those are layer 4. No release fraction is invented for a nuclide that has no quoted released activity.
